fig1.title: Appliance Energy Consumption Distribution
fig1.observation: Heavily right-skewed distribution with long tail. Base standby load is around 50 Wh, with active appliance usage spiking up to 1080 Wh.
fig1.implication: Evaluation must report MAE (robust to long tail) alongside RMSE (penalizes large peak errors). Standard linear regression assumes normality of errors.

fig2.title: Energy Consumption Over Time
fig2.observation: Data spans Jan 11, 2016 to May 27, 2016. Seasonal transition from winter to spring reduces heating and lighting requirements.
fig2.implication: Requires chronological splitting. Random splitting would cause future seasonal trends to leak into training models.

fig3.title: Average Consumption by Hour of Day
fig3.observation: Pronounced diurnal cycle with morning rise (~8 AM) and evening peak around 18:00 reaching 190.4 Wh. Night trough at 3:00 drops to 48.2 Wh.
fig3.implication: Time-of-day and cyclical encodings (sin_hour, cos_hour) are foundational features.

fig4.title: Consumption Patterns by Day of Week
fig4.observation: Slightly higher consumption on weekends (Saturday/Sunday) due to sustained residential occupancy and domestic chores.
fig4.implication: Weekend indicator and day-of-week cyclical encodings are essential indicators of occupant presence.

fig5.title: Temperature versus Energy Consumption
fig5.observation: Direct linear correlation between raw ambient temperature and instantaneous appliance consumption is modest (~0.05 - 0.10), because appliance spikes are event-driven rather than continuous thermodynamic loads.
fig5.implication: Nonlinear algorithms (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) are superior to simple linear relationships.

fig6.title: Humidity versus Energy Consumption
fig6.observation: Indoor humidity (RH_1) exhibits positive association during cooking/dishwashing events due to steam generation. Outdoor humidity correlates negatively with appliance use.
fig6.implication: Humidity measurements reflect indoor activities that generate both moisture and electricity draw.

fig7.title: Correlation Heatmap
fig7.observation: High multicollinearity between internal temperatures (T1 and T2 correlate at r=0.88). Random noise variable rv1 correlates with target at r=-0.01 (pure noise).
fig7.implication: High sensor collinearity impairs ordinary least squares regression without regularization. rv1 and rv2 must be discarded. Tree-based ensembles are resilient to collinear features.

fig8.title: High-Consumption Events and Outliers
fig8.observation: Peak spikes typically last for 20 to 60 minutes (2 to 6 consecutive 10-minute intervals), characteristic of standard washing, drying, or cooking cycles.
fig8.implication: Lagged features (10m, 20m, 30m) and short-term rolling statistics provide critical temporal continuity to anticipate the duration of active cycles.

fig9.title: Weather-Related Relationships
fig9.observation: Outdoor meteorological features show non-linear and weak direct correlation with momentary appliance draws, but reflect macro-weather conditions that govern household routines.
fig9.implication: Outdoor variables serve as secondary contextual indicators rather than primary drivers.

fig10.title: Target Distribution & Log-Scale Transform
fig10.observation: Original target has high skewness (3.39). Log transformation reduces skewness to 1.19, consolidating the multimodal peaks around standby and typical active usage.
fig10.implication: Linear models benefit from log-scale training, while tree-based ensembles handle skewed continuous targets naturally.
